extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, social scientists, historians, and students of social-science methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing, verifying, and using generalizations (empirical and scientific) in the social sciences, including how to combine historical evidence with laws of human nature and how to infer conditions for stable political societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from history without grounding in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Never introduce any generalization from history into the social science unless sufficient grounds can be pointed out for it in human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historical order of succession, even if regular, is only an empirical law unless it can be connected with psychological and ethological laws on which it depends; without that connection it cannot be relied on for prediction beyond adjacent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from scientific laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws (generalizations from history) are not scientific laws until connected with the laws of human nature and supported by consilience of deduction a priori with historical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical generalizations can guide inquiry but must be converted into scientific theorems by showing they follow from elementary principles of human nature; otherwise their predictive power is severely limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constantly verify historical generalizations by psychological and ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The only check or corrective on erroneous historical generalizations is constant verification by psychological and ethological laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such verification, mistaken empirical laws will continually be made; compare historical-derived laws with what is expected from human nature to raise evidence toward proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require domain competence for preparing historical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: No one but a person competently skilled in the laws of human nature is capable of preparing the materials for historical generalization by analyzing historical facts or observing social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent persons know which facts are comparatively important, what to observe, and how to infer evidence from indirect marks; others risk misestimating evidence and producing erroneous laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize two kinds of empirical laws: co-existence and succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical Laws of Society are of two kinds: uniformities of co-existence and uniformities of succession; these correspond to Social Statics and Social Dynamics respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Social Statics to study conditions of stability (consensus among social elements) and Social Dynamics to study laws of progress; the distinction mirrors mechanics (equilibrium vs movement) and biology (organization vs life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Social Statics to infer contemporaneous relations when direct observation is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: The statical branch allows us to infer one social element from others (subject to verification) similarly to how anatomy infers conditions of parts by their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can substitute for direct observation of some elements; but one must estimate limits of variation and avoid exaggerating simplicity of relations to prevent error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to obtain empirical laws of correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain better empirical laws, combine the statical view (simultaneous conditions) with the dynamical (successive order) to derive laws of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law of correspondence, duly verified a priori, would become the real scientific derivative law of human development; consider both the contemporaneous condition and progressive changes of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a predominant social element to serve as the central explanatory chain
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one social element is pre-eminent it can serve as the central chain to which other progressions attach, simplifying the empirical ordering of historical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History and human-nature considerations show the state of speculative faculties (the state of knowledge and prevailing beliefs) is such a predominant element; use progression of ideas/knowledge as the central axis linking other social changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about a priori prediction of long historical series
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not generally possible to determine a priori the long order of human development because long series of actions and reactions are too complex and small errors amplify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if elementary laws suggest a sequence, the sheer length and interdependence of links makes exact computation by human faculties impracticable; thus rely on empirical verification and limit predictions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of empirical laws derived from few instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws often result from but a few instances because few nations attain high stages of progress independently; such small samples make empirical laws unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one or two pivotal instances are imperfectly known or poorly compared, wrong empirical laws will emerge; ensure thorough analysis and comparison before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inverse-deductive verification where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: After an empirical law is suggested by history, attempt to demonstrate a priori that such an order was to be expected (inverse deductive method) as a real process of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often one can only show strong a priori reasons for expecting a given order, not uniqueness; inverse deduction complements empirical verification and is indispensable when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always consider mutual interdependence of social elements (the 'consensus')
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element of the social state must be considered relatively to all other elements, with which it is united by mutual interdependence; their necessary relations permit inference of one from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consensus allows inferring contemporaneous states across sciences and arts; but because social interdependence is complex, estimation of variation limits (healthy vs morbid) is essential to avoid error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify requisites of stable political union by comparative analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: By comparing different societies, one can find requisites present where social union is most complete — conditions without which a state ceases or reconstructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such requisites are empirical but some, when supported by human-nature laws, rise to scientific truths; examples include laws/tribunals/organized force, education, allegiance, and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education with restraining discipline as a condition of stable society
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of education beginning in infancy and continued through life, with restraining discipline to subordinate impulses to societal ends, is a principal requisite for durable political society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education trains individuals to subordinate personal aims to societal ends and control disruptive feelings; relaxation of this discipline correlates with social disorganization, anarchy, or decline into despotism or conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a feeling of allegiance or loyalty (a fixed point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Durable societies exhibit a feeling of allegiance or loyalty—some settled, unquestioned point (to gods, persons, laws, or principles) that is held sacred and not casually disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fixed point prevents internal dissension from becoming civil war; habitual questioning of fundamental principles undermines stability; the form of allegiance may vary with culture and institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of cohesion or sympathy among members (not hostile nationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong active principle of cohesion—a feeling of common interest and sympathy among members of the same community—is essential for lasting political society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not xenophobic nationalism but union and shared identity (one people); absence of this feeling (regionalism, weak national sentiment) leads to fragmentation or foreign domination, as illustrated by historical examples.
